title: India Charts ₹10,000-Crore Waterway and Container Plan to Slash Logistics Costs
excerpt: The 2026-27 Budget commits to 20 new national waterways, a domestic container manufacturing ecosystem, and a dedicated freight corridor linking eastern and western India.
body:
• India's Budget 2026-27 allocates ₹10,000 crore over five years to build a domestic container manufacturing ecosystem, reducing near-total dependence on Chinese imports.
  • The government will operationalize 20 new national waterways and launch a Coastal Cargo Promotion Scheme to double waterway transport's share from 6% to 12% by 2047.
  • A new Dankuni-to-Surat Dedicated Freight Corridor will connect eastern mineral belts to western ports, complementing the inland waterway expansion.
  • Ship-repair ecosystems in Varanasi and Patna, along with regional training centres, will support the infrastructure buildout across the Gangetic plain.

A Strategic Pivot to Water and Rail

India's freight network has long been hostage to its roads. Trucks carry roughly 65% of the country's cargo, pushing logistics costs to nearly 14% of GDP — among the highest of any major economy and well above the 8-10% typical of developed nations. The 2026-27 Union Budget, presented by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, attempts to change that equation with a sweeping ₹10,000-crore investment in waterways and container infrastructure.

https://x.com/DoC_GoI/status/2088912241156661383

The centrepiece is a five-year scheme to create a "globally competitive" container manufacturing industry. India currently produces about 30,000 shipping containers a year. China makes six million. That gap leaves Indian exporters exposed to price shocks and supply disruptions every time global shipping tightens — a vulnerability that the Covid-era container crisis and the more recent Strait of Hormuz disruption made painfully clear.

"The bulk of India's logistics cost disadvantage stems not from distance but from modal imbalance — too much on road, too little on water and rail."

— Industry analysis, Rising India News

20 New Waterways, Starting With Odisha

Alongside the container push, the government will operationalize 20 new national waterways over the next five years. The rollout begins with NW-5 in Odisha, connecting the mineral-rich areas of Talcher and Angul and industrial hubs like Kalinga Nagar to the ports of Paradeep and Dhamra. The route is designed to move bulk commodities — coal, steel, fertilizers — off congested rail corridors and onto barges at a fraction of the cost.

A Coastal Cargo Promotion Scheme will incentivize shippers to move freight from road and rail to coastal and inland routes. The target: raise waterway transport's share from 6% to 12% by 2047. That may sound modest, but India's inland waterways currently carry less than 2% of total freight. Reaching even 5% would be a generational shift, according to the Inland Waterways Authority of India.

Ship-repair ecosystems are planned for Varanasi and Patna, addressing a basic infrastructure gap. India has hundreds of inland vessels but limited maintenance capacity along key rivers. Regional training centres will also be established along the waterway routes, creating employment in states like Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, and West Bengal.

The Freight Corridor Link

The waterway plan is paired with a new Dedicated Freight Corridor from Dankuni in West Bengal to Surat in Gujarat. The corridor will complement India's existing Eastern and Western freight corridors by connecting mineral-producing eastern districts to manufacturing and port hubs in the west. For the inland waterway network to work at scale, last-mile connectivity between river terminals and rail or road networks is essential — a lesson India learned the hard way from the slow ramp-up of the Varanasi-to-Kolkata stretch on the Ganga.

Customs reform is also part of the package. A single digital window for cargo clearances, expanded bonded warehousing, and duty deferrals for Authorised Economic Operators are designed to trim invisible costs from logistics chains. Faster clearances reduce dwell time at ports and airports, directly benefiting freight forwarders and exporters handling time-sensitive goods.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs investing in Indian manufacturing or logistics, the waterway and container push signals a structural cost reduction that could improve margins across industries from steel to pharmaceuticals. Companies listed on Indian exchanges with exposure to logistics infrastructure — Container Corporation of India, Adani Ports, and inland vessel operators — saw positive market responses after the Budget announcement.

What to Watch

The plan's success hinges on execution. India has announced national waterway expansions before — 111 rivers were declared national waterways in 2016, but most remain unnavigable for commercial traffic. Last-mile connectivity, port handling efficiency, and cargo aggregation have historically lagged behind headline announcements. The five-year timeline will face its first real test when NW-5 in Odisha begins handling commercial cargo, expected within the next 12-18 months.
